title: Bugs Bunny
description: Cartoon character; mascot of Warner Bros.
wiki_lead:
Bugs Bunny is a cartoon character created in the late 1930s at Warner Bros. Cartoons (originally Leon Schlesinger Productions) and voiced originally by Mel Blanc. Bugs is best known for his featured roles in the Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies series of animated short films, released by Warner Bros. Pictures. Earlier iterations of the character first began appearing in Ben Hardaway's Porky's Hare Hunt (1938). Hardaway refined the character until Tex Avery's A Wild Hare (1940) introduced his definitive characteristics. He was given the name Bugs Bunny in Elmer's Pet Rabbit (1941). Bob Givens, Chuck Jones, and Robert McKimson are credited for defining Bugs's visual design.
Bugs is an anthropomorphic gray-and-white rabbit or hare who is characterized by his flippant, insouciant personality, his Brooklyn accent, and his catchphrase "Eh... What's up, doc?". He is typically portrayed as a trickster, outwitting foes like Elmer Fudd and Yosemite Sam as well as various authority figures and criminals. He develops a friendly rivalry with Daffy Duck. Through his popularity during the golden age of American animation, Bugs became an American cultural icon and Warner Bros.' official mascot.
Bugs starred in more than 160 short films produced between 1940 and 1964. He has since appeared in feature films, television shows, comics, and other media. He has appeared in more films than any other cartoon character, is the ninth most-portrayed film personality in the world and has his own star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

Development

According to Chase Craig, who wrote and drew the first Bugs Bunny comic Sunday pages and the first Bugs comic book, "Bugs was not the creation of any one man; however, he rather represented the creative talents of perhaps five or six directors and many cartoon writers including Charlie Thorson. In those days, the stories were often the work of a group who suggested various gags, bounced them around and finalized them in a joint story conference." A prototype Bugs rabbit with some of the personality of a finalized Bugs, though looking very different, was originally featured in the film Porky's Hare Hunt, released on April 30, 1938. It was directed by Ben "Bugs" Hardaway. This cartoon has an almost identical plot to Avery's Porky's Duck Hunt (1937), which had introduced Daffy Duck. Porky Pig is again cast as a hunter tracking a silly prey who is more interested in driving his pursuer insane and less interested in escaping. Hare Hunt replaces the little black duck with a small white rabbit. According to Friz Freleng, Hardaway and Dalton had decided to "dress the duck in a rabbit suit". The white rabbit had an oval head and a shapeless body. In characterization, he was "a rural buffoon". Mel Blanc gave the character a voice and laugh much like those he later used for Woody Woodpecker. He was loud, zany with a goofy, guttural laugh. grok_lead: Bugs Bunny is an anthropomorphic cartoon rabbit character created for Warner Bros.' Merrie Melodies animated shorts, first officially appearing in the 1940 film A Wild Hare, directed by Tex Avery. The character, designed as a wisecracking trickster who habitually chews carrots and utters the catchphrase "What's up, Doc?", was primarily voiced by Mel Blanc, whose versatile performances defined Bugs' sassy Brooklyn-esque persona from the debut onward. Introduced during the Golden Age of American animation, Bugs Bunny quickly became the central figure of the Looney Tunes franchise, starring in hundreds of theatrical shorts where he outmaneuvers dim-witted hunters like Elmer Fudd through cunning disguises, anachronistic references, and psychological taunts rather than physical combat. His debut short established the core dynamic of verbal sparring and fourth-wall breaks that propelled the series' popularity, leading to Bugs supplanting earlier rabbit prototypes and embodying Warner Bros. Cartoons ' irreverent house style under producers like Leon Schlesinger. Bugs Bunny's cultural impact includes a sole Academy Award win for the short Knighty Knight Bugs (1958) in the category of Best Short Subject (Cartoons), alongside nominations for earlier entries like A Wild Hare, cementing his status as a benchmark for animated comedy. The character's enduring legacy spans television revivals, feature films such as Space Jam (1996), and modern adaptations, with voice successors like Jeff Bergman maintaining Blanc's template amid shifts in animation techniques from hand-drawn cels to digital formats.
